results.answer: 3M's FY2018 capital expenditure was $1,577 million, shown as "Purchases of property, plant and equipment (PP&E)" of (1,577) in the 2018 Consolidated Statement of Cash Flows (years ended December 31, 2018). This is the cash outflow for PP&E purchases, which the cash flow statement records as capex.
3M's year-end FY2018 net PP&E was $8.738 billion (USD millions 8,738: gross PP&E $24,873M less accumulated depreciation $16,135M), as reported on the Consolidated Balance Sheet at December 31, 2018.

Moderately, not heavily. In FY2022 3M spent $1,749M on PP&E purchases against $34,229M of net sales (about 5.1%), and net PP&E of $9,178M was about 19.8% of $46,455M total assets (net PP&E is about 27% of sales). Capex was about 0.96x depreciation and amortization ($1,831M), so it is roughly maintenance-level reinvestment with little expansion. These ratios describe a manufacturer with a meaningful but not dominant fixed-asset base; the library does not give an industry benchmark, so the label is my judgment from these ratios.

3M's GAAP total-company operating margin fell from 20.8% in 2021 to 19.1% in 2022 (-1.7 pts), with operating income down 11.3% to $6,539M on sales down 3.2% to $34,229M. The drop was driven mainly by special items, chiefly the $2,291M significant-litigation costs (Combat Arms Earplugs) and the $800M PFAS manufacturing exit charge, partly offset by a $2,724M gain on the Food Safety/Neogen divestiture. Excluding special items, adjusted margin fell from 22.2% to 20.8% (-1.4 pts), with underlying pressure from raw material and logistics costs and manufacturing productivity headwinds, partly offset by selling price actions and restructuring. Operating margin is a useful metric for 3M (the 10-K reports it at total and segment level), but GAAP margin is distorted by large special items, so the adjusted figure is needed to see the underlying trend.

Consumer. In 2022, excluding M&A (acquisitions contributed 0% to every segment, and divestitures are a separate line), 3M's organic sales grew 1.2% company-wide. Consumer was the only segment with negative organic growth, at -0.9%, while Safety and Industrial grew 1.0%, Transportation and Electronics 1.2%, and Health Care 3.2%. Consumer's total sales change was -3.9%, including -0.4% from divestitures and -2.6% from translation.

Yes, the quick ratio is a relevant liquidity measure for 3M, but it does not indicate a clearly healthy position at June 30, 2023. Quick ratio = (cash $4,258M + marketable securities $56M + accounts receivable $4,947M) / total current liabilities $10,936M = 9,261 / 10,936 ≈ 0.85x. That is below 1.0x, meaning quick assets do not fully cover current liabilities without inventory or prepaids; the broader current ratio is 15,754 / 10,936 ≈ 1.44x, and the 0.85x figure is a tighter view. Short-term borrowings rose to $3,033M from $1,938M at December 31, 2022.

As of Q2 2023 (quarter ended June 30, 2023), 3M's registered debt securities under Section 12(b) are three notes, all listed on the New York Stock Exchange: 1.500% Notes due 2026 (MMM26), 1.750% Notes due 2030 (MMM30), and 1.500% Notes due 2031 (MMM31). The cover page lists these alongside common stock, which is not a debt security.

Yes. 3M's cash dividends paid per share rose every year in the filings read: $2.54 (2013), $3.42 (2014), $4.10 (2015), $4.44 (2016), $4.70 (2017), $5.44 (2018). In Feb 2019 the board declared a $1.44 quarterly dividend, up 6%, its 61st consecutive year of increases. The one dip is in declared dividends for 2015 ($3.075 vs. $3.59 in 2014), which reflects timing: the Q1 2015 dividend was declared in December 2014, so 2015 declarations covered only three quarters.

FY2019 fixed asset turnover ≈ 24.26x. Total net revenues were $6,489M in FY2019, and average net PP&E was $267.5M ((253 + 282) / 2, with $253M at Dec 31, 2019 and $282M at Dec 31, 2018), so 6,489 / 267.5 = 24.26.

Activision Blizzard's FY2017–FY2019 average capex as a % of revenue is 1.9%. Capex (purchases of property/equipment in the cash flow statement) divided by total net revenues from the statement of operations was 2.2% for FY2017 ($155M / $7,017M), 1.7% for FY2018 ($131M / $7,500M), and 1.8% for FY2019 ($116M / $6,489M), averaging 1.9%.

FY2015 operating cash flow ratio = 1,469,502 / 2,213,556 = 0.66 (in thousands). Net cash provided by operating activities was $1,469,502K for the year ended November 27, 2015, and total current liabilities at that date were $2,213,556K.

Adobe's operating income rose 65.4% year over year, from $903,095K in FY2015 to $1,493,602K in FY2016 (($1,493,602 − $903,095) / $903,095 ≈ 65.4%), per the reported GAAP Consolidated Statement of Income.

FY2017 operating cash flow ratio ≈ 0.83. Net cash provided by operating activities was $2,912,853K and total current liabilities at December 1, 2017 were $3,527,457K, so 2,912,853 / 3,527,457 = 0.8258, rounded to 0.83 (figures in thousands, as reported).

No. Adobe's FY2022 operating margin did not improve. It was 34.6% in FY2022 (operating income $6,098M / revenue $17,606M), down from 36.8% in FY2021 ($5,802M / $15,785M), a decline of about 2.1 points. It is above FY2020's 32.9% ($4,237M / $12,868M), so the trend is mixed over the period. Operating margin is a useful metric for Adobe: it reports one operating income line and its expenses are reported in the same income statement. The FY2022 decline reflects operating expenses rising 15% (R&D +18%, S&M +15%, G&A +12%) faster than revenue (+12%).

Yes. Computing free cash flow as operating cash flow minus purchases of property and equipment, and dividing by net income, conversion rose from about 101% in FY2020 to about 143% in FY2021 and about 155% in FY2022. FY2022 FCF was $7,396M ($7,838M - $442M) against net income of $4,756M; FY2021 was $6,882M ($7,230M - $348M) against $4,822M; FY2020 was $5,308M ($5,727M - $419M) against $5,260M. Adobe's 10-K does not report an FCF conversion metric, so this ratio is my calculation from the cash flow statement; the rising ratio is driven by operating cash flow growing faster than net income, mainly from deferred revenue.

0. AES Corporation's FY2022 Consolidated Statements of Operations has no restructuring line item (the lines run from revenue and cost of sales through G&A, interest, impairments, and other non-operating items, with no restructuring entry), so restructuring costs are not explicitly outlined on the income statement.

AES sold (turned over) its inventory roughly 12 times in FY2022. Using cost of sales of $10,069M and average inventory of $829.5M ((1,055 + 604) / 2), the turnover ratio is about 12.1x (about 30 days). On year-end inventory of $1,055M it is about 9.5x. Conventional inventory turnover is only of limited meaning for AES: its cost of sales includes depreciation, O&M, G&A, bad debt and derivative gains/losses, not just inventory consumed, and inventory (mainly fuel, raw materials and spare parts) is small at about 2.7% of total assets ($1,055M of $38,363M). The ratio is therefore a rough indicator, not a true sell-through measure.

ROA ≈ -1.42% (-0.01 as a decimal). FY2022 net income (loss) was $(505)M, the consolidated 'NET INCOME (LOSS)' line. Average total assets were $35,663M ((38,363 + 32,963) / 2), so -505 / 35,663 = -0.0142. Net loss attributable to AES was $(546)M, which would give about -1.53%.

Amazon's FY2017 DPO is 93.86 days. Average accounts payable is (25,309 + 34,616) / 2 = 29,962.5 million. FY2017 cost of sales is 111,934 million, and the change in inventory is 16,047 − 11,461 = 4,586 million, so the denominator is 116,520 million. DPO = 365 × 29,962.5 / 116,520 = 93.86 days, using the balance sheet's accounts payable and inventories and the income statement's cost of sales as the question specifies.
Amazon's total net sales rose 30.8% from FY2016 to FY2017: ($177,866M − $135,987M) / $135,987M = 30.8%, using the 'Total net sales' line of the Consolidated Statements of Operations.

$11,588 million. The FY2019 income statement reports Net income of $11,588M and no noncontrolling-interest line, so net income equals net income attributable to shareholders. Check: basic EPS of $23.46 × 494M basic shares ≈ $11,590M, consistent with this figure.

Amcor's FY2020 year-end net trade receivables were $1,615.9 million (as of June 30, 2020), taken directly from the Consolidated Balance Sheet line 'Trade receivables, net'; this is down from $1,864.3 million at June 30, 2019. The balance sheet shows no separate AR line, so this is the net AR figure used.

The Amcor plc Form 8-K dated July 1, 2022 (event date June 30, 2022) reported a single item, Item 8.01 Other Events, with no financial results or other agenda items. On June 30, 2022, Amcor Finance (USA), Inc. (former issuer) and Amcor Flexibles North America, Inc. (substitute issuer), both wholly-owned subsidiaries of Amcor plc, entered into a Second Supplemental Indenture under the 2016 Indenture and a First Supplemental Indenture under the 2019 Indenture. Together they substitute Amcor Flexibles North America for Amcor Finance (USA) as issuer of the 3.625% Guaranteed Senior Notes due 2026 and 4.500% Guaranteed Senior Notes due 2028, and the substitute issuer assumes the former issuer's covenants.

Improved. Using the conventional quick ratio, (current assets − inventories) ÷ current liabilities, FY2023 is 3,095 ÷ 4,476 ≈ 0.69x, up from FY2022's 3,414 ÷ 5,103 ≈ 0.67x. The stricter cash + receivables ÷ current liabilities also rose, from 0.53x to 0.57x. The quick ratio is a reasonable liquidity metric to ask about Amcor, since it carries large inventories, but analysts usually pair it with the current ratio and net debt/EBITDA. Inventories fell from 2,439 to 2,213 and current liabilities fell from 5,103 to 4,476, so the ratio improved even though current assets dropped from 5,853 to 5,308.

FY2023: three acquisitions. (1) Aug 1, 2022: 100% of a Czech Republic flexible packaging plant company, $59M consideration (later identified as DGPack s.r.o. in the Q2 FY2023 10-Q); (2) Mar 17, 2023: 100% of a medical device packaging site in Shanghai, China, $60M including $20M contingent consideration; (3) May 31, 2023: a New Zealand manufacturer of automated protein packaging machines, $45M including $13M contingent consideration. Total about $164M. FY2022 and FY2021: no acquisitions are disclosed. Their acquisition/divestiture notes list only divestitures (FY2022: non-core Flexibles asset disposals; FY2021: a European hospital supplies business, India and Argentina non-core businesses, and the AMVIG stake). The Bemis acquisition (June 11, 2019) falls in FY2019, not FY2021–FY2022.

Amcor operates in the packaging industry. It describes itself as a global leader in developing and producing responsible packaging for food, beverage, pharmaceutical, medical, home and personal-care, and other consumer goods end markets, offering flexible packaging, rigid packaging containers, specialty cartons, and closures across two segments (Flexibles and Rigid Packaging).

No. Amcor's gross margin fell in FY2023, so the profile is not improving. Gross profit was $2,725M on net sales of $14,694M (18.5%), down from $2,820M on $14,544M (19.4%) in FY2022, and from $2,732M on $12,861M (21.2%) in FY2021. The 10-K attributes the decline mainly to the pass-through of higher raw material costs and to disposed operations. Gross margin is still a usable metric for Amcor, a manufacturer of flexible and rigid packaging with cost of sales of about 81% of revenue. The pass-through effect means the margin percentage moves with resin and other raw-material prices, so it understates the underlying operating performance, which the 10-K describes as favorable operating cost performance.

At December 31, 2022 (end of Q2 FY2023), Amcor's restructuring plan liability was $93 million: $81M employee costs, $2M fixed asset-related costs and $10M other costs. It is an accrual for unpaid restructuring costs, mainly from the Russia-Ukraine conflict restructuring and, to a lesser extent, the 2019 Bemis integration plan. The company expects most of it to be paid within twelve months, and it is recorded in other current and non-current liabilities. The liability rolled forward from $118M at June 30, 2022, with $2M of net charges, $25M of cash paid and $2M of unused amounts reversed.

Amcor's fiscal 2023 (twelve months ended June 30, 2023) Adjusted EBITDA was $2,018 million, down from $2,117 million in fiscal 2022 (about -5%). The reconciliation table shows adjusted EBITDA of $2,018M for the twelve months ended June 30, 2023, after starting from reported EBITDA of $2,080M and adding back the non-GAAP items.

Approximately 0% (flat). For fiscal 2023 vs FY2022, Amcor's comparable constant-currency growth in total net sales is "—" (nil). Reported net sales rose 1% (14,694 vs 14,544, $ million). Stripping out FX (-3 pts), raw material pass-through (+5 pts) and items affecting comparability (-1 pt) leaves 4 - 5 + 1 = 0%. The volume (-3%) and price/mix (+3%) components net to the same 0%.

FY2015 D&A margin ≈ 4.18%: D&A of $167M (cash flow statement) ÷ FY2015 net revenue of $3,991M (statement of operations) = 4.18%. The cash flow statement is the source for D&A, and the income statement is the source for revenue, so the margin uses the two statements as the question asks.

Yes, on the quick ratio. At Dec 31, 2022, AMD's quick assets were $9,981M (cash and equivalents $4,835M + short-term investments $1,020M + accounts receivable, net $4,126M), against total current liabilities of $6,369M, giving a quick ratio of about 1.57x (up from about 1.49x at Dec 25, 2021: $6,314M / $4,240M). Quick ratio is a relevant liquidity measure here because it excludes inventories ($3,771M) and prepaid/other current assets ($1,265M), which are less readily convertible to cash; a ratio above 1.0x means liquid assets cover current liabilities.

As of FY22, AMD sells its products across four segments. Data Center: AMD EPYC server CPUs, Instinct GPU accelerators, Xilinx FPGAs/Adaptive SoCs and Alveo accelerator cards, and Pensando DPUs. Client: Ryzen and Athlon desktop and notebook CPUs, Ryzen PRO/Threadripper PRO commercial CPUs, and chipsets (X670, B650, X570, etc.). Gaming: Radeon discrete GPUs (RX 7000/6000 series, Radeon PRO workstation GPUs) and semi-custom SoCs for PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X|S and Steam Deck. Embedded: embedded EPYC CPUs, Ryzen Embedded V- and R-Series APUs, and embedded FPGAs/Adaptive SoCs with development kits. This is stated in the product sections of the FY22 10-K, which list each product family under its segment.

AMD's total net revenue rose from $16,434M in 2021 to $23,601M in 2022, an increase of $7,167M (about 44%). The increase was driven mainly by Embedded, up $4,306M from $246M to $4,552M because of the Xilinx acquisition (closed February 2022), and Data Center, up $2,349M from $3,694M to $6,043M on higher EPYC server processor sales. Gaming rose $1,198M on higher semi-custom console SoC demand. Client fell $686M (about 10%) on a 24% drop in unit shipments, partly offset by a 19% rise in average selling price.

AMD's operating margin fell from about 22.2% in FY21 (operating income $3,648M on $16,434M revenue) to about 5.4% in FY22 (operating income $1,264M on $23,601M revenue), a drop of roughly 17 percentage points. The decline was driven mainly by amortization of acquisition-related intangibles from the Xilinx and Pensando deals (about $3.5B: $1.4B in cost of sales and $2.1B in operating expense), plus higher R&D (+$2.2B) and MG&A (+$888M), which outweighed 44% revenue growth. Operating margin is a useful metric for AMD, but the FY22 figure is heavily distorted by acquisition accounting, so the underlying operating performance is better read with that amortization excluded. Margin figures are my calculations from the reported numbers.

Operations brought in the most cash in AMD's FY2022 (year ended December 31, 2022): operating activities provided $3,565 million, versus investing activities provided $1,999 million and financing activities used $3,264 million. Operating cash flow was the largest positive contributor and the only one of the three that was a source of cash larger than the others; financing was the largest outflow.

Data Center. Excluding Embedded, Data Center net revenue rose from $3,694M in FY21 to $6,043M in FY22, up about 63.6%, versus Gaming at about +21.4% ($5,607M to $6,805M) and Client at about -10.0% ($6,887M to $6,201M). Data Center had the largest proportional increase.

Yes. AMD's FY2022 annual report (year ended December 31, 2022) discloses two major customers, each at least 10% of consolidated net revenue: Customer A at 16% (Gaming segment) and Customer B below 10% in 2022 (11% in 2021, Client segment). This is disclosed as a major-customer table in the segment note, which shows the concentration.

None. The American Express Company 2022 Form 10-K (fiscal year ended Dec 31, 2022) lists only one security under Section 12(b): Common Shares (par value $0.20), trading symbol AXP, on the New York Stock Exchange. The cover page also states 'Securities registered pursuant to section 12(g) of the Act: None.' No debt securities are shown as registered on a national exchange; the 10-K's exhibit 4.1 says the long-term debt instruments are omitted under Item 601(b)(4)(iii)(A) of Regulation S-K.

American Express's 2022 geographic operations are the United States, EMEA (Europe, Middle East and Africa), APAC (Asia Pacific, Australia and New Zealand), and LACC (Latin America, Canada and the Caribbean). The United States dominated in 2022, with $41,396M of the $52,862M total revenues net of interest expense (about 78%), versus $4,871M for EMEA, $3,835M for APAC and $2,917M for LACC; the company itself frames its segments as primarily United States versus outside the United States.

No. On the proxy pretax margin, 2022 is down from 2021 but up from 2020. Pretax income divided by total revenues net of interest expense was 18.1% in 2022 (9,585 / 52,862), versus 25.2% in 2021 (10,689 / 42,380) and 11.9% in 2020 (4,296 / 36,087). Measured after credit-loss provisions (50,680 / 43,799 / 31,357 for 2022 / 2021 / 2020), the pattern is the same: 18.9%, 24.4% and 13.7%. Operating margin is not a reported or useful metric here: AMEX's consolidated income statement has no operating-income line, and as a card issuer with a bank funding model its interest expense is an operating cost inside revenue, so pretax margin on net revenue is the closest measure. The 2022 decline is driven by higher Card Member rewards (14,002 vs 11,007), marketing and salaries, and by provisions swinging to a 2,182 charge from a 1,419 reserve release in 2021.

Gross margin is not a useful metric for American Express and is not reported: the income statement has no cost-of-sales or gross profit line, because AmEx is a card issuer and network whose costs are interest, Card Member rewards, provisions for credit losses, and operating expenses. The FY2022 pretax-income change was driven by revenue growth outpacing expenses: total revenues net of interest expense rose $10,482M (25%) to $52,862M, led by discount revenue (+$6,176M) and interest income (+$3,625M), but total expenses rose $7,985M (24%) to $41,095M, led by Card Member rewards (+$2,995M) and business development (+$1,181M), and provisions for credit losses swung from a $1,419M release to a $2,182M charge. Pretax income fell 10% to $9,585M from $10,689M, and net income fell to $7,514M from $8,060M. For reference only, my own proxy of revenues net of interest expense less Card Member rewards gives 73.5% in 2022 versus 74.0% in 2021 (computed, not reported by the company).

American Express's effective tax rate fell by 3.0 percentage points, from 24.6% in FY2021 to 21.6% in FY2022. The 10-K attributes the decline mainly to discrete tax benefits in 2022 from resolving prior-year tax items.

Customer deposits were the largest liability on American Express's 2022 Consolidated Balance Sheet at $110,239 million (about $110.2 billion), ahead of total other liabilities ($37,350M, the next-largest line), long-term debt ($42,573M), accounts payable ($12,133M) and short-term borrowings ($1,348M). Justification: it is the largest single line item among the liabilities reported on that statement.

Yes. The 2022 10-K says Card Member retention "remained high" in 2022, and net card fees rose 17% year-over-year as new card acquisitions reached record levels. The filing gives no numeric retention or attrition rate, so "able to retain" rests on this qualitative statement.
American Water Works paid $389 million in cash dividends in FY2020, or about $0.389 billion. The consolidated statement of cash flows shows 'Dividends paid' of (389) for 2020, up from (353) in 2019.

FY2021 unadjusted EBITDA for American Water Works is $1,832 million: operating income of $1,196M from the income statement plus depreciation and amortization of $636M from the cash flow statement (which matches the income statement's D&A line).

No. At December 31, 2022, American Water Works had negative working capital of about $(1,561) million: total current assets of $1,250M less total current liabilities of $2,811M. The main driver is short-term debt of $1,175M, plus a current portion of long-term debt of $281M. Working capital is computable from the balance sheet, so the metric applies here.

FY2015–FY2017 3-year average net profit margin ≈ 2.8%. Net profit margin = net earnings attributable to Best Buy shareholders ÷ revenue: FY2017 1,228/39,403 = 3.12%; FY2016 897/39,528 = 2.27%; FY2015 1,233/40,339 = 3.06%; average = 2.81%. Justification: taken from the FY2017 10-K consolidated statements of earnings (revenue and net earnings for each of the three fiscal years). Using net earnings including noncontrolling interests gives the same 2.8%.
$5,409 million. Best Buy's FY2019 10-K consolidated balance sheet (fiscal year ended February 2, 2019) reports Merchandise inventories of $5,409 million, the FY2019 year-end figure.

Yes, on a percentage-point basis. Consolidated gross profit as a % of revenue ran 22.4% (FY2015), 23.3% (FY2016), 24.0% (FY2017), 23.4% (FY2018), 23.2% (FY2019), 23.0% (FY2020), 22.4% (FY2021), 22.5% (FY2022), and 21.4% (FY2023). Year-over-year moves were +0.9, +0.7, -0.6, -0.2, -0.2, -0.6, +0.1 and -1.1 points, so no single year moved more than about 1.1 points. Gross margin is a relevant metric for Best Buy, which reports it as a headline consolidated figure and discusses it in MD&A. Caveat: if the 2% threshold is read as a relative change rather than percentage points, FY2023 (-4.9%), FY2016 (+4.0%) and FY2017 (+3.0%) exceed it. FY2024 and FY2025 annual figures were not found in the library, so the series ends at FY2023.

FY2023: no acquisitions are disclosed in the FY2023 10-K. FY2022: two, Current Health Ltd. (care-at-home technology, closed Nov 2, 2021, $389M net cash) and Two Peaks, LLC d/b/a Yardbird Furniture (direct-to-consumer outdoor furniture, closed Nov 4, 2021, $79M net cash). FY2021: none. The FY2021 10-K acquisitions note lists only earlier deals, GreatCall (FY2019), and CST and BioSensics (FY2020). Justification: the FY2023 10-K's acquisitions note covers only the FY2022 deals, and the FY2021 10-K's acquisitions note lists no FY2021 deal.

Operations brought in the most cash in FY2023: operating activities provided $1,824M, versus investing activities using $962M and financing activities using $1,806M. Operating cash flow was the only positive contributor, while investing (-$962M) lost less than financing (-$1,806M).

Yes. Best Buy's cash and cash equivalents fell from $1,874M at FY2023 year-end (January 28, 2023) to $1,093M at Q2 FY2024 (July 29, 2023), a decrease of $781M (about 41.7%). The 10-Q attributes the decline to inventory purchases and payments, dividends, and capital expenditures, partly offset by earnings. Best Buy was the company I matched to the question, since the question does not name one.

Yes, the count fell. At the end of Q2 fiscal 2024 (July 29, 2023) Best Buy-branded U.S. stores (Domestic segment) numbered 907, down from 930 at the end of Q2 fiscal 2023 (July 30, 2022), a decrease of 23. Including Canadian Best Buy stores (128 vs. 127), Best Buy-branded stores went from 1,057 to 1,035 (-22). Across all Domestic and International stores, the total fell from 1,142 to 1,129 (-13). This comes from the Q2 FY2024 10-Q store roll-forward tables, which show the closures and openings in each period.

Computing and Mobile Phones was the top Domestic (USA) category in Q2 FY2024 (quarter ended July 29, 2023), with $3,674M of revenue, or 41% of the $8,890M Domestic total, ahead of Consumer Electronics at $2,658M. It was the largest category by revenue in the 10-Q's product-category table.

Working capital ratio ≈ 1.73 (FY2016 total current assets $1,001,425K ÷ total current liabilities $577,464K = 1.734, rounded to 1.73). Both figures are from Square, Inc.'s (Block) consolidated balance sheet as of December 31, 2016.

101.5%. Total net revenue rose from $4,713,500K in FY2019 to $9,497,578K in FY2020, so growth = (9,497,578 − 4,713,500) / 4,713,500 ≈ 101.5%. The income statement shows this increase, driven mainly by Bitcoin revenue ($516,465K to $4,571,543K) alongside growth in transaction-based and subscription revenue.

Block (Square, Inc.) generated $381.6 million in net cash provided by operating activities in FY2020 ($381,603 thousand). This is the figure in the FY2020 10-K consolidated statement of cash flows, and the MD&A cash flow table reports the same amount.

Boeing's net property, plant and equipment at December 31, 2018 was $12,645 million, per the Consolidated Statements of Financial Position, which lists it as a separate balance sheet line (up from $12,672 million in 2017).

Yes. Three of Boeing's reportable segments each exceed 20% of FY2022 total revenues of $66,608M: Commercial Airplanes $25,867M (38.8%), Defense, Space & Security $23,162M (34.8%), and Global Services $17,611M (26.4%). Boeing Capital ($199M, 0.3%) and unallocated items/eliminations (−$231M) do not. The 10-K reports revenue by these segments, which are organized by products and services, and does not give a finer product/service dollar split, so the test was applied to segments.

Yes. Boeing's FY2022 10-K (Note 21, Legal Proceedings) discloses two ongoing matters it singles out, both with no estimable loss range: (1) remaining lawsuits from the Lion Air Flight 610 and Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 accidents and the 737 MAX, where the company says it cannot reasonably estimate losses not covered by insurance; and (2) an arbitration with Embraer over the terminated 2019 joint-venture agreements, expected to finish in late 2023 or early 2024. The note says its general belief that proceedings will not have a material effect applies 'except as described below,' so these two are the matters it flags as potentially significant. Its 2022 settlements (a $219 shareholder derivative recovery received in Q2 2022 and a $200 SEC civil penalty paid in October 2022) are resolved, not ongoing.

Yes, but only modestly, and only on a derived basis. Boeing does not report gross margin itself. Computing it as total revenues minus cost of products and cost of services from the consolidated statement of operations: 2022 gross profit is $3,530M on $66,608M revenue (5.3%), up from $3,049M on $62,286M (4.9%) in 2021, and sharply up from a loss of $5,642M (-9.7%) in 2020. The roughly 40 bps gain is thin and driven by program accounting. Gross margin is a weak metric for Boeing because reach-forward losses and abnormal production costs flow through cost of products, and 2022 still ended with a $3,547M loss from operations, so operating and core-loss measures are more informative.

Boeing's primary customers in FY2022 are commercial airlines (the Commercial Airplanes segment sells principally to the commercial airline industry worldwide) and the U.S. government (including foreign military sales). U.S. government revenue was 40% of FY2022 consolidated revenue of $66,608M. Non-U.S. customers accounted for $27,374M and U.S. customers for $39,218M. The 10-K states Boeing derives a significant portion of its revenue from a limited number of commercial airlines.

Yes. Boeing's 10-K states that the airline industry 'has been cyclical and very competitive and has experienced significant profit swings,' and that demand for its commercial aircraft and services is driven by airline profitability, traffic growth, and macroeconomic conditions. Significant deterioration in the global economy or the airline industry could reduce orders and deliveries, so the business is cyclical through its dependence on airline demand (stated in the FY2021 10-K; the same language appears in the FY2019 10-K).

Cross currency swaps had the highest notional value among Verizon's FY2021 derivatives used to manage foreign currency and interest rate exposure, at $32,502 million at December 31, 2021 (versus $19,779M for interest rate swaps, $1,000M for forward starting interest rate swaps, and $932M for foreign exchange forwards). The notional-amounts table lists these four instruments as its outstanding derivatives.

As of the FY2021 10-K, Verizon expected benefit payments to retirees in 2024 of $1,097 million for pension benefits and $862 million for health care and life, a total of $1,959 million. The table in the FY2021 10-K's "Estimated Future Benefit Payments" section lists these expected 2024 amounts by benefit type.

Verizon's FY2022 quick ratio is about 0.54x: (cash $2,605M + accounts receivable, net $24,506M) / total current liabilities $50,171M = $27,111M / $50,171M. A ratio below 1.0 means quick assets do not cover current liabilities, so on this measure alone Verizon does not look strongly liquid. The quick ratio is still a relevant measure for Verizon, but it should be read with its cash generation: operating cash flow was $37,141M in 2022, and current liabilities include $9,963M of debt maturing within one year. The filing gives no marketable securities line, so the calculation excludes them.

Yes. In FY2022 Verizon spent $23,087M on capital expenditures (including capitalized software), about 16.9% of its $136,835M total operating revenues ($23,087 / $136,835). That is about 1.35x its $17,099M depreciation and amortization, and capex absorbed about 62% of its $37,141M operating cash flow, leaving $14,054M of free cash flow. Heavy ongoing network investment relative to revenue and cash flow makes it capital intensive.

No. Verizon's balance-sheet debt fell slightly in 2022. Total debt (current plus long-term, including commercial paper) was $150,639M at Dec 31, 2022, versus $150,868M at Dec 31, 2021, a decrease of $229M (about 0.2%). Long-term debt dropped from $143,425M to $140,676M, while debt maturing within one year rose from $7,443M to $9,963M; the decline in long-term debt more than offset the rise in current debt.

FY2018 DPO for Walmart ≈ 42.69 days. Average accounts payable = (46,092 + 41,433) / 2 = 43,762.5; COGS FY2018 = 373,396; change in inventory = 43,783 − 43,046 = 737; DPO = 365 × 43,762.5 / (373,396 + 737) = 15,973,312.5 / 374,133 = 42.69. Inputs come from the FY2018 consolidated income statement (cost of sales) and consolidated balance sheet (accounts payable, inventories) in the Walmart FY2018 10-K, in $ millions.

The FY2018→FY2019 change in unadjusted operating income margin is +0.2 percentage points. Operating margin on total revenues rose from 4.1% (20,437 / 500,343 = 4.08%) in FY2018 to 4.3% (21,957 / 514,405 = 4.27%) in FY2019, based on the consolidated statement of income in the FY2019 10-K.

FY2018–FY2020 3-year average unadjusted EBITDA margin for Walmart is 6.2%. Unadjusted EBITDA (operating income + D&A) over total revenues was 6.02% (FY2020), 6.34% (FY2019) and 6.19% (FY2018), giving a simple average of 6.19%, which rounds to 6.2%. Using net sales as the denominator also rounds to 6.2%. Inputs: operating income 20,568 / 21,957 / 20,437 and D&A 10,987 / 10,678 / 10,529 ($ millions).
